I know you have nothing to add to this. If you add anything to it in your style it will detract from it. Every hon. member within the sound of my voice knows why it was done. The kindliness of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, who is always very kind, prevented him from telling you why. He knows that his own province of British Columbia only produces 10 per cent of their beef requirements. He quite properly said today: Why should we be forced to accept beef until we know that our wildlife and our dairy cattle of the Fraser valley are secure? Why should 

members from the province of Quebec accept them? It is true it might temporarily help the beef producers of the province of Ontario to be able to send beef to the province of Quebec, but right at the present time, when there is a little suspicion concerning two or three districts in the province of Ontario, I do not blame the province of Quebec for saying that they are going to wait until they are sure that they can import healthy animals from the other provinces. They at least have the sovereign right to prevent it and they are going to prevent it.
But without coming to parliament, without asking those of us who represent the people, three hours in advance of the meeting of the house today the Minister of Agriculture says that he will ban the importation of beef. He may think that the Ontario beef producers and farmers on the back concession lines will think he is working with them but the people of British Columbia and Quebec will know so well that the only purpose it could serve would be to starve them into submission and make them accept beef whether or not they thought it was dangerous. It does nothing so far as helping the beef producers of Canada is concerned.
The market is shot anyway but for a few weeks the province of Quebec can certainly get its beefsteaks and other beef, which they can well afford to buy. They can get beef for their lumber camps, beef for their fancy hotels in Quebec City and Montreal in the same way as other provinces that have plenty of beef. As the hon. member for Fraser Valley knows, British Columbia can get its beef from the United States at least for a few months until this thing settles down. But now, on twenty-four hours' notice and outside of parliament, the Minister of Agriculture announces that we will stop beef coming into Canada knowing that beef will not come into Ontario anyway but preventing it from coming into Quebec and British Columbia so as to starve the people there into submission. If you do not let United States meat in you will eat Newfoundland flippers or something else instead of roast beef.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: A fate worse than death.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
The Dominion of Canada has rapidly been growing into a great storehouse of purebred livestock. In the last few years we have produced more high-class livestock and increased our production to a greater extent than any other country in the world. France, Belgium, the Argentine, with the drought she has suffered in the last while, and other countries in South America are

very glad to import. During the last five years I am satisfied that from my riding at least $75,000 worth of dairy cattle have gone to South America alone, to say nothing of the great volume that goes across the border every week into the United States. Now we know that overnight that market is prohibited. We know that overnight the value of the purebred herds in the province of Ontario is almost cut in half.
How long is it going to take to recover? You will recall that I mentioned the Fordney-McCumber tariff and the Hawley-Smoot tariff. They were put into effect because the United States had too much beef at the time, and they thought they could protect the livestock men of Oklahoma, Texas, and other American states. They never had an excuse like this. I venture to say that, while it is to be in effect for sixty days, it will be difficult to remove, and the removal will not be made easier by the fact that we have made such a clumsy explanation of how the disaster started and how it was handled in Canada. I think that it not only means a death blow to the great basic industry of agriculture, the livestock industry, but it is the greatest discouragement to the livestock producers of Canada in the last half century. The discouragement does not arise particularly because of the fact that we have been contaminated with the dreaded foot-and-mouth disease. I am not so much concerned with that now because after you have a wreck there is not much use in talking about who hit you. You had better get your hospital bills paid and get straightened out. I am not so much concerned about that. As the hon. member for Lake Centre said so well this afternoon, you have chased an immigrant up and down this country from Montreal to Fort William and back to Montreal and finally found him in Vancouver. By now you have probably inspected his clothing, his boots and his hat, and found out where he has been. It may be that he worked on a farm in Holland, Belgium, Poland or Germany that was contaminated with foot-and-mouth disease, which we know is prevalent over there. I think the Minister of Agriculture might ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration whether the immigration officers who are selecting those who come to Canada are experienced men. He might ask him whether his immigration inspectors do anything about it when they find a group of young farmers coming from an area infected with foot-and-mouth disease, particularly when we know that even in Mexico when coming out of the infected 55704-5
Foot-and-mouth disease areas people are required to drive their automobiles through a chemical solution so they will not carry the disease.

speechtext: The hon. member apparently was not in the house this evening when the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration dealt with that matter and announced that they were taking action.

I am glad they have begun to take action, but apparently that has been done just recently. I know the department has called back from Europe some immigration officers who apparently were not serving as efficiently as the department considered they should. I am wondering just how loose this whole machinery may be. All down the line we have had what goes with a government that has a top-heavy majority and a top-heavy civil service, a bureaucracy that is almost tumbling over itself. The government has a Pollyanna complacency that often results in the errors and mistakes that I am trying to point out; and I say that in all kindliness.
I venture to believe that in his heart of hearts the right hon. minister knows there must have been some laxity in his department. Nothing I have heard yet convinces me that there has not been carelessness, complacency, a disregard for facts and even worse in ithe Department of Agriculture, to permit this situation to develop though it had sufficient warning three months ago. It is not good enough for the minister to say he spoke to Tom Jones or Bill Smith or somebody else in Calgary, even though they are personal friends of his and excellent citizens, as they all are out there, and that because they did not mention it to him his responsibility ended.
The minister says a quarantine was set up. If that were so, why were Mr. Waas' children allowed to go to school without missing a day? Why were the people of that district allowed to go in to do their shopping, to tramp through the stores and be followed by men and women from farms in other districts? If a quarantine was set up that meant anything at all why were they permitted to send dozens of carloads of cattle to Ontario and. Quebec, and to St. Paul in the United States? Where is the section you are going to extend by fifty miles and slaughter all the cattle in order to increase the area of your quarantine? You had better go fifty miles out from St. Paul, or fifty miles out from London, Ontario. Do you blame the people of British Columbia or the people of Quebec for being a little dubious when they know that during January and February cattle were shipped to Ontario and Quebec from the very district that was supposed to be under quarantine?
66	HOUSE OF
Foot-and-mouth disease
What assurance have we as livestock dealers in this country that we are going to be protected in future? I have always understood that no one could bring animals across the border without a careful inspection. For fifty years we have never thought of foot-and-mouth disease being imported into this country from the United States. If our veterinary authorities are not able to diagnose foot-and-mouth disease in less than three months what assurance have we that cattle which have been imported from the United States are not diseased? Were the veterinarians at the border smarter than the veterinarians in western Canada? Were they smarter than Dr. Childs or Dr. Mitchell or the other men who should get their heads together and find out what has been going on?	.
I leave this thought with the Minister of Agriculture, and no one in this house will grasp its significance more quickly. If the United States put a ban on our livestock going to that country because of foot-and-mouth disease, they will not be liable to lift it any sooner if some congressmen can say that we had foot-and-mouth disease in Canada for three months before we knew it. Stop and think over that one. A congressman can say the records shovf that on November 26 we had a disease that looked so much like foot-and-mouth disease that the local veterinaries could not distinguish it. Because of the lackadaisical attitude and the complacency of the Department of Agriculture and the veterinary service of Canada, for whatever reason they did not diagnose it as foot-and-mouth disease, nor did they diagnose it as anything else. I know for a fact farmers in that district asked the veterinaries whether this could possibly be foot-and-mouth disease, so it was talked about. In one respect I must say the minister may have been right. I have read some of the speeches made in western Canada by those who were familiar with this matter, and I know the local veterinaries generally considered that it must be only vesicular stomatitis. But when the farmers generally became inquisitive and asked for an investigation, as a national responsibility, as a national duty, as something vital to the economy of this country concerning this basic industry, surely there should have been an investigation. Surely samples should have been sent to Regina or Saskatoon or Hull to make sure that it was vesicular stomatitis rather than foot-and-mouth disease. To my mind that was a careless evasion of responsibility on the part of someone in this country which will mean a great deal as the years go by.


I do not like to stand idly by and watch this country become a secondary livestock producing country. We have the facilities for growing grain and fodder to feed great herds of livestock. We have markets, and we have developed industry in this country. We have great home markets, and there are great markets opening every year overseas to restock the herds that were depleted during the recent war. To find those markets shut off at a time when our economy is slipping, and to find that it has happened without the Department of Agriculture knowing their business or perhaps being careless in the administration of a responsibility to the economy of this country, is quite a shock.
I do not know that I can add much to this issue except to say that I well recall the surpluses of 1932. I can well recall talking in those years about the importance of the livestock industry. I recall some hon. members from western Canada saying that we would never see wheat below $1.25 per bushel, yet I remember it selling for 40 cents and even lower in some districts. I remember when the Hawley-Smoot tariff closed our cattle from United States markets. This is the third time the United States has closed us out of their market. The great champions who sit to your right, Mr. Chairman, who were to find the United States market and hold it forever, and who thought it was so much more important than the British market, find that this is the third time the United States has closed its market to Canadian cattle.
In 1932 everyone in this house was concerned about where we would find markets. May I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that since the United States has Closed this market and with more reason than they had before, while we have complacently allowed a dangerous disease to spread through our cattle for three months until now it has spread to God knows where, at least he should take definite steps to find a market for the surplus cattle. Instead of worrying too much about what we may receive for the infected animals, we ought to find countries that have had foot-and-mouth disease to whom we could send animals under proper inspection. If we are going to be left in a position that looks dark, I suggest that the government should meet and decide whether or not it would be wise to appropriate substantial funds to get this surplus beef out of Canada, even if it has to be given away. We could make sure that none of the infected carcasses go outside the country.
I will not use the word "cowardly", but I will say that I do not think it is a very game way of dealing with an issue, to ban products

from the United States of America, with all the international complications of retaliation and so on. It is our problem, so do not blame it on the United States. Do not try to starve the people of the province of Quebec or the people of British Columbia. They are entitled to their provincial autonomy. So far as the province of Ontario is concerned, it does not make much difference because no cattle will enter at 12 cents per pound less. Quebec should not be forced to buy Ontario or any other beef until they are ready to do so.

Perhaps I can give it now in greater detail than I could have given it previously. In the first place, the idea is being built up that somebody discovered foot-and-mouth disease on the farm of Mr. Waas or on the farm of Mr. Smith, who lived in the same area, or on the farm of some three or four others who lived around Mr. Waas. No, his cattle have not been shot. Some of them may be tomorrow, but they have not been shot yet. It has not been established that foot-and-mouth disease has been on the farm of Mr. Waas. As a matter of fact, Mr. Waas called in a veterinarian for the first time on November 26 to consult him about a disease which his animals had. As I stated the other night, his veterinarian was sick and was not able to go, but he did prescribe for this disease known as stomatitis. The animals recovered.
At a later date, I think it was demonstrated today that that date was about December 2, Mr. Waas became somewhat concerned about something and he sent into Regina for members of our veterinary staff.
Foot-and-mouth disease I think one of the members went out that day and one on a later day, probably the next day. Altogether Mr. Waas and his neighbours had seven different veterinarians in that district examining their cattle during the latter part of November and the early part of December. Every one of the seven veterinarians said it was not foot-and-mouth disease. It is my understanding that by the 5th of January these men were relieved of any idea that there had been foot-and-mouth disease on their farms.
So far as anyone knows, that would have been the end of the matter had the disease not broken out somewhere else. The disease was discovered, not on anyone's farm, but in the packing plant of the Burns Company at Regina. When it was discovered there-

The disease did break out in the Regina plant of Burns, in so far as we are certain, and might not have broken out on the farm of Mr. Waas at all. The only reason for thinking that it has any association with Mr. Waas is that, seven days before any of his animals were infected with any disease, he delivered livestock to the Burns plant in Regina. It was only after discovery was made of some traces of the disease as leading back to the plant at Regina that thought was given to Mr. Waas and his neighbours. These particular cattle of his were traced back to his farm, of course, and it was found that he had this other disease there. Investigations have been carried on

Foot-and-mouth disease there since; but his cattle have not yet been destroyed. That situation has some bearing on the fact that this immigrant has been followed here and there up and down the country. It leaves a different interpretation on the question as to what you would find if you found traces of a virus being carried by this particular individual on his clothes, on his boots or in some other way. It would prove one thing, in all probability, namely, that there is a possibility that animals were afflicted with that disease on the farm of Mr. Waas. It would not necessarily prove that he brought the disease from Germany to this country but it might prove that he himself contacted animals on that place while he was there; and he was there, I think, about a week or a week and a half before these animals were delivered to the Burns plant. That circumstance might suggest that he had been in contact on that farm, in one way or another, with animals that developed the foot-and-mouth disease. Hence, for every reason, the department should follow this matter through to the bitter end and find out if there is any reason for believing that this immigrant was in any way associated with the disease, either on the farm of Mr. Waas or in Germany before he came here, or that he was a carrier of the disease.
I think that leaves a different picture with regard to the situation as related to Mr. Waas. If nothing else had happened except what happened on the Waas farm and in his neighbourhood, I am quite satisfied that we would not be having this discussion tonight at all; because that particular livestock had been treated, and to all intents and purposes had been cured. Moreover, I understand that there has not been any further outbreak on that particular farm. That situation, of course, could change from day to day. Because of the fear that there might have been some association there, the government is going so far as to destroy those herds; but before we destroy them, we should like to determine whether or not we have got to the source of the disease. We are not at all certain that we have done so. Seven different veterinarians said it was not foot-and-mouth disease. Some of them were our representatives. Some of them were veterinarians practising in the community. I am not sure whether any of them were provincial men. In any event there were seven different veterinarians who were called there and who gave the opinion that it was not foot-and-mouth disease.
I am quite prepared to say that I was pleased indeed to listen to the remarks made by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth


this afternoon. I think he did all members a great service as he certainly did me. He gave me, with regard to the disease, information which I did not have and I thank him for it. But at the same time I am quite prepared to take the opinion of seven veterinarians out in the Regina district, who visited the area and saw the livestock, in preference to the opinion of a veterinarian sitting in this house as to whether or not those animals had foot-and-mouth disease.

They had foot-and-mouth disease in the United States in 23 different states. My hon. friends know that right up until just a few years ago, as a matter of fact, to about the time that I came into this department, we were denied the right to ship any stock to Britain for any other purpose than for slaughter because there had been foot-and-mouth disease in the United States, not because there was foot-and-mouth disease in this country. In other words, if you shipped a carload of steers and heifers over to Glasgow they had to be slaughtered within a certain period of time and sold as beef. You could not leave the heifers there as breeding stock. The same thing applied if they went to Manchester or London. They were denied the opportunity of going into that country for a period of well over thirty years, I think. We were denied the right to go to Britain because they had foot-and-mouth disease in the United States. That was largely owing to the fact that they did not feel that we could prevent it from coming across the boundary line, judging by their experiences, as has been said. It was not a Liberal government that was in power over many of these years. Over many of these years a Conservative government was in power. But over all the years, those who were labouring in the departments of agriculture, either provincial or federal, under
[Mr. Gardiner.!

these governments did succeed in keeping foot-and-mouth disease out of this country. But that did not stop the British from saying that because it was on this continent they would not take our breeding stock.
That brings us down to just a few years ago. Now, with regard to our United States friends and their position with relation to the whole matter: They took 404,000 head of cattle, either in butchered form or live weight, last year. Why are they going to be worrying about the export market into Canada for cattle and beef? They are going to be worrying about the fact that they are to be short 404,000 head of cattle in the United States this year because we have foot-and-mouth disease.

Foot-and-mouth disease
My hon. friend has said, and quite properly, that the meat-producing section of the agricultural industry is one of the greatest sections in that industry. We depend upon it for our existence more than we do upon anything else. I think everyone will agree that it is important that the people have a market somewhere for their product, and the only place they can have a market, for the time being, is in the Dominion of Canada.
This government is concerned with seeing to it that the people in all parts of Canada are given as much protection as they possibly can have against having the disease transferred to their areas from the area in which it is now located. That is what we are concerned about. And I can only repeat what I said over the radio this morning- and, by the way, I make no apology for having said it over the radio. In the first place, the house did not meet this morning and, in the second place, the markets to which we were talking opened at about nine o'clock. It must be remembered that eleven o'clock here is nine o'clock in western Canada. It did mean something to the farmers in those areas to know at nine o'clock this morning what the position was, rather than have to wait until this afternoon to find it out. And I am sure they would be a long time finding it out, if they had to wait for the kind of discussion we have had tonight.
With that in mind we took the course that I indicated on Friday we probably would take when it became necessary to do anything in connection with this matter. I pointed out that we would do it in the quickest possible way, and get it into operation just as soon as possible. That was done.
Let me repeat that our main objective in doing what we did was to see to it that the farmers did have one market; and we are hopeful that the other things announced this morning will result in that market being able to handle the beef, pork, mutton and lamb which does go to the market in Canada. That is our main objective. We think what we have announced will accomplish this. And I am quite satisfied that what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Melfort- and may I say I was somewhat surprised someone did not say it before he did, in view of the sources from which much of the criticism has been coming-is worthy of careful consideration. He said he is quite satisfied that if we do not deal with these men fairly we will have to stand criticism. I am quite satisfied, too, that that is so. If we do not

Foot-and-mouth disease deal fairly with the farmers, those who are having their animals slaughtered, we will have to take criticism.
This makes it important, first, that we see to it that they are treated fairly and, secondly, that we do not allow this to lead us into spending too much of the taxpayers' money in taking care of the situation. We ought to spend what is absolutely essential in order to treat these people fairly, but on the other hand we should not spend any more than is absolutely necessary to treat them fairly. And so we have set up an organization which we think will take care of both of those objectives, namely, that of treating them fairly while, at the same time, seeing to it that we do not waste the money of the people of Canada in doing so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? I was under the impression that he was going to tell us about some authority who had come over from the United States.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member mentioned that. I had so many questions from all sides that, at times, I get off on some other tack. One of these men who came over from the United States to help us made a speech in Winnipeg or Regina, I am not sure which it was, on either Friday or Saturday night. In that speech he called attention to a few facts. One statement he made was that the disease had been in 23 states in the United States, and he congratulated the people of Canada, the government of this country and all those concerned with the disease upon the fact that; we had caught it before it had got beyond a district no larger than fifty miles square.
He emphasized the fact that if we could hold it there and stamp it out from that small area we would be conferring a service not only upon this country but upon the whole continent. I am satisfied that that is so. And so we have set up an organization which will do exactly that about which some people a few moments ago were smiling.
Whether we can prove absolutely that cases which had been diagnosed as stomatitis were, in fact, foot-and-mouth disease, we intend to destroy the animals that had that other disease, or that were diagnosed as having had it. And we believe we are doing a service not only to the men concerned but to all Canada in seeing to it that no chance whatsoever is taken in connection with a matter of that kind, and that the animals are destroyed.
I think I should say we also have a duty toward those individuals. That duty does not end with the destruction of their livestock. If their buildings are polluted with

the disease, they will be destroyed, too. We have got to be fairly sure when we begin destroying livestock that they have the disease. If it is absolutely established that they have it, then we will have a lot more expense than merely the expense of paying for the animals slaughtered.
I do not think anyone will suggest that we should be in too big a hurry to destroy animals within an area, so long as it is tightly quarantined. When no one has diagnosed the disease that was on a farm as being the foot-and-mouth disease, we should not be in too big a hurry if we can find any way of establishing that the disease was never there. Because these men all have equipment which they are very anxious should not be destroyed. They know it cannot be replaced by the expenditure of equal sums of money, or sums equal to those for which the equipment was purchased.
We have to be careful about it-and we are being careful. I would say once again I do not think we are helping the situation by suggesting that someone was lacking in his enthusiasm to take care of the disease in its early stages. Everyone was following it as closely as they could and no one diagnosed the case as foot-and-mouth disease until the month of February. Therefore while there might be criticism for our officials not having acted maybe two weeks earlier than they did-and I say "officials" because the government had no reason for believing there was foot-and-mouth disease there-on the other hand when persons are saying six weeks or three months earlier that is an entirely different thing. I do not think any evidence has been established anywhere that anyone was lacking in judgment or administrative ability between the 26th day of November and at least the latter part of the month of January. There might be some criticisms about what happened after that. However, we can hear those as we go along, and probably anything we have to say with regard to them will also be removed when we hear the evidence before the committee.
My friend immediately across from me said a little while ago that the price of cattle had gone down 12 cents. I don't know. It depends upon what area you are talking about. Cattle prices have gone down considerably in some places and not so much in others. If the situation is allowed to remain as it is at present I am afraid there are just as many areas in Canada where the price will go up as there are where it will go down. Where it goes up it will go up to abnormal heights and where it goes down it will go down to unreasonable levels unless someone does something about it. But I do want to

suggest and I do not think the government or all the taxpayers of Canada should assume the full responsibility for what may be done by very limited sections of Canada.
The suggestion has been made that great good may be done to some areas by eliminating livestock from those areas, but the fact is that some of the areas that have been mentioned do not get livestock in any considerable numbers. Much of the beef that has been talked about tonight is actually killed in Winnipeg now to be sent to some parts of eastern Canada. The amount which goes as livestock and is killed in some of our larger city areas is not nearly so great as has been suggested. Much of that meat is killed in western Canada. I want to emphasize what I said this afternoon, namely, that there is sufficient packing house capacity on the prairies to kill all the livestock that come to market there. There is sufficient packing house capacity there to kill not only all that comes now but there was sufficient to kill the runs that were going during wartime. At that time we had them all in operation to 100 per cent of their capacity. They have never been in operation to 100 per cent of their capacity since, and if the remainder of Canada says that all the livestock produced in western Canada must be killed there they are not doing any harm to western Canada. Western Canada is not going to kick about that. It will give employment to far more men than are employed now in western Canada.
My friends from the Regina area and my friend from Winnipeg have been a little concerned about paying the men who are out of jobs for the moment in the city of Regina. There is far more likelihood of their having jobs and having increased time if we go on as we are now than there is of their being without jobs.

We will get that as we go along. You do not settle these things overnight. What I am suggesting is that there are some other parts of Canada where there may be
Foot-and-mouth disease unemployment in some plants because they have not the livestock to kill. If there is, that is not a problem which we created. It is a problem which someone else created. I want to emphasize once more that livestock in western Canada is just, as secure from foot-and-mouth disease as any livestock you can find anywhere in the world. Since it is in that position there is no reason why it should not be transferred elsewhere and slaughtered, thus keeping the plants busy that have been slaughtering livestock in the years gone by. We are not going to do anything which is going to prevent that happening, but we are going to see to it that all livestock that comes to market whether east or west, whether on the prairies or somewhere else, is killed and put into shape where it can be marketed in some market somewhere. If we find we have meat which ought to go somewhere we can then consider the methods under which we may send it to Britain or elsewhere, but for the time being we are concerned about maintaining this market for our own livestock since it is the only one we know we have got. Then we are concerned next about going out and finding every market we can for our meat in any form, and we are probably in just as good a bargaining position with our boundary closed as we would be if it were in any other condition.
We hope to be able to deal with the matter on that basis and proceed to solve the problems associated with it. We do not anticipate any trouble with our United States friends. We think they are satisfied with the battle we are putting up. They think we are going to be successful. They think we are going to be able to show that this disease can be stamped out in that small area, and we are going to try to prove to them that that is the case and stamp it out. If we do I hope all parts of Canada will co-operate with us ini seeing to it that in the meantime our meat products are consumed on the Canadian market to the greatest extent possible. I think that necessitates our stopping the scaring of people with respect to this matter. A loti of people have the feeling that if one of these animals that have come within a thousand miles of the city of Regina lands in some other part of the world everybody in the community is going to have their livestock affected with foot-and-mouth disease.
As a matter of fact I have had telephone calls from Calgary within the last twenty-four hours suggesting that I appeal to the housewife and tell her that there is not a chance in the world of this meat affecting human beings. It is suggested that I do that because they are stopping their buying and are not taking the meat into their homes. I think we

Foot-and-mouth disease should stop the scaring of people all over the country in that way and get down to dealing with the matter in a common sense way. I think the common sense way at the moment is to pass the bill and put us in a position to go out and make payments. If my hon. friends are not satisfied let me say that they will know all about it by next Friday. We will be paying the bills throughout this week. I think we will still be debating the speech from the throne next Friday, and there is no reason in the world why any hon. member should not bring forward any grievances that anyone has as to the payments that are made with respect to their livestock. There is no reason why he should not bring them up on the floor of the house and discuss them, but I venture to say that there will not be very many put forward, that the people will be satisfied with the treatment they receive from the government, and that they will feel it is fair. What we are suggesting is that this legislation provides for fair and reasonable payment, and I am quite satisfied that nine out of ten of the people who are interested and concerned are also satisfied that this thing ought to be given a trial and that they will get fair treatment when it is given on that trial.

speechtext: This is my first opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to say anything on this matter. I assure you I will not emulate the minister's marathon and somewhat circuitous remarks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: I only spoke for twenty minutes. If you equal that you will be all right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
As the minister has said, we have been fortunate in that so far this outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease has been confined to a relatively small area in Saskatchewan. I also agree with the minister that any alarm that may be felt by housewives and others in regard to the meat they take home should be allayed as quickly as possible, and that the minister and all the rest of us should do whatever is within our power to put the minds of the people at rest in regard to any danger from that source.
There may be some reason to believe that the disease has been contained within a comparatively small area in Saskatchewan; but that may be due to the weather. This outbreak occurred during the winter, when things of that kind do not spread nearly as rapidly as in warmer weather when flies and birds are about. So I do not think for one moment we should consider the problem with any feeling of complacency, in the belief that it has been contained within a small area and everything is fine. When the weather gets

warmer it may well spread very quickly, and certainly every precaution should be taken to see that this does not happen.
While up to the present the disease has not spread very far, the economic repercussions as far as the livestock industry is concerned have been extremely serious. I am afraid they will be even more serious, and may disastrously affect the entire economic life of the country. I do not like to be repetitious, and I am not going to be; but I cannot understand the delay of nearly three months in making a laboratory test in connection with the outbreak of this disease. The more the minister talked a few minutes ago, the more he went around and around in connection with the Waas farm and what was done and what was not done, the more confused the situation became. I would like to ask him whether in actual fact, as I understand from what he has said, even yet no laboratory test has been made to determine whether the Waas cattle had foot-and-mouth disease. It seems entirely inconceivable that this should be the situation, but the minister says the cattle have not been shot yet and we do not know whether they had foot-and-mouth disease.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: I am sorry if I did not make the situation clear. The disease was diagnosed as stomatitis. That was in December, and by January 6 they were clear of any disease. It is impossible to go and test those cattle. I think my hon. friend will agree that when the disease is not in the animals at all there is no way of checking the virus, because the virus is not there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I do not know much about the medical or veterinarian end of it, but as I understand it this disease remains in the marrow of the bones of the cattle and can be transmitted for a very considerable time afterward. So it seems that it would still be possible to make laboratory tests to determine whether they had it and still carry it.
This afternoon and again this evening the minister referred at some length to the quarantine which was put into operation. According to my understanding that quarantine is really not very effective, and a considerable number of the farmers in the area concerned have no great confidence in it. I understand that the people within the quarantined area have been going into McLean and other towns quite readily, and their children have been going to school. This has all been going on ever since this disease first broke out, and it is still going on. So as far as any close quarantine is concerned, it just does not exist. It seems to me that perhaps the most serious aspect of this affair as far as the spread of the disease is concerned is the fact that it was present at this plant and these stockyards, and that cattle were shipped from there to various parts of Canada and the United States.
Another point in connection with the spread of the disease on which I have not heard anything so far is whether any steps have been taken or are contemplated, or can be taken, to prevent the spread of the disease up and down the Qu'Appelle river valley through the deer and other wildlife in that area. I do not know whether there is any other wildlife but deer, but it seems to me one of the greatest dangers in connection with the spread of the disease right across the country, once warm weather comes, is in connection with the wildlife, because from the Qu'Appelle valley it could quite easily spread by that means to every other valley in western Canada, and from there right across eastern Canada, and into British Columbia in the other direction. It seems to me some steps should be taken to ensure that this does not happen, because as I have seen the present quarantined area outlined on the map it goes right into the Qu'Appelle valley.
A great deal has been said about the various embargoes that have been imposed. We in the prairie provinces are in the unfortunate position of having embargoes against us in every direction, with the result that we have no place to go with our cattle or the meat produced from them. That being so, the price of cattle in the prairie provinces might drop to almost nothing, as the minister well knows. In this bill mention is made of fair and reasonable compensation. I trust that if the livestock market in the prairie provinces should collapse completely, whatever the going price might be would not be considered fair and reasonable compensation for the cattle which may have to be slaughtered. As a matter of fact there is a certain danger in the other direction as well. It may be that our situation as far as markets are concerned 55704-6i
Foot-and-mouth disease will become such that people will be glad to have their cattle condemned in order to get a market for them. That may be so if these embargoes continue for any length of time and we have no place to ship our cattle.
Floor prices have been mentioned. Generally speaking I have not been a very great proponent of floor prices in this house or outside it, or of the control of the agricultural economy or any other part of our economy. That is my position under ordinary circumstances. However, this is anything but an ordinary circumstance, and I believe there is every justification for floor prices under livestock of all sorts in order to protect the producers of western Canada. If necessary the surplus should be taken off the market by the dominion government and shipped overseas as a contribution to those countries which are badly in need of food.
Even the floor price which exists today is not working very well. The floor price on hogs is $26. The price actually being paid in Calgary for grade A hogs on Thursday was $22, that was $4 below the floor price which applies in Toronto. Why there should be this spread of $4 I do not know, but perhaps that is another question the minister may be able to answer when he speaks again. Certainly, there is no use putting in a floor price if it does not operate any better than that floor price does so far as the Alberta hog producers are concerned.
It seems to me that the whole embargo question is one which should be reconsidered by the people who placed those embargoes in effect, perhaps without the panic thinking which caused them to be put into operation. I would hope that after greater consideration some of these embargoes might be removed.

There is nothing secret and mysterious about biological warfare. It's not a super-weapon against which there's no defence. There is plenty of defence, and scientists are at work every day planning preventive measures. For instance, they have developed a fluid which makes people immune or resistant to the well-known poison, botulism, . . . There are other people engaged in taking precautions against the people who might try to spread germs or poisons.
Industrial engineers know that saboteurs could cripple a war plant by spraying biological agents through the ventilation system, so they have devised special protection against that. If any suspicion arises that some form of biological warfare is being waged, every civil defence organization in Canada is ready to give information, issue instructions and go into action . . .

speechtext: The whole matter will be considered, but I cannot tell the hon. member what the government policy is until it is settled.

workers who, through no fault of their own, are unemployed? We are prepared to agree to reimburse the farmers who have lost their income. Why should we not be prepared to help the workers in the packing house industry who, for the same reason, are losing their income? Surely this is a matter of equity and justice.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
And, Mr. Chairman, that is typical of the kind of remark that has delayed proceedings all day. It is precisely like the
Foot-and-mouth disease old melodrama that probably the minister himself has seen, where two people are fighting a duel on the stage. One of them is being sorely pressed, and he says to the other, "Look at yon wandering crow"-and then the fellow looks up while the one who spoke sticks him.
And that is exactly the type of argument being carried on by the minister. He has scarcely answered a single question directly today. That is the reason the matter is still under discussion-and there is no other reason.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: That is not the reason.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
That is the reason. The Minister of Agriculture has not made any effort to explain one perfectly simple fact, or to answer one perfectly simple question. This is not some obscure tropical disease that is unknown to the veterinarians of Canada. This is a disease recognized as one of the dangerous diseases that must be checked and must be diagnosed in its earliest stages.
We have great veterinary colleges in Canada. We have great veterinarians. The simple fact is that the statement that this disease cannot be diagnosed without serum is sheer and unadulterated nonsense. If that were so we would have no protection in this country against the importation of animals carrying this disease. We have always supposed this was being carefully guarded against at all times. If we need this serum in Canada to discern the disease, then procure it elsewhere. We should have the serum in Canada. We have great laboratories here. We have the Banting institute in Toronto.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
There are international
regulations with regard to it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
There is no difficulty about having our research institutions provide whatever serum of this kind is required. And, in any event, we are only a matter of twelve or fourteen hours away from the English supply, if it is needed. Either we need to keep the serum here for a purpose of this kind, or we should produce it here ourselves.
But if the minister's explanation is correct, that there is nothing surprising about not being able to diagnose this within three months, then any suggestion that we really afford protection at our borders against the possibility of diseased animals coming in, and bringing in foot-and-mouth disease, is sheer and unadulterated pretence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: That is not my contention.

speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
We have before us tonight the suggestion that there is nothing surprising about a delay of three months in diagnosing a disease that has been known for many long years, and in regard to which graduate veterinarians from every veterinary college in this and other countries are well trained.

Would the minister suggest that if a doctor failed to diagnose some well-known disease in human beings there would be no reason for criticism? In this particular case there has been gross negligence somewhere. Instead of going around in circles and putting up a smokescreen such as we have seen today at a time when the people of this country are so greatly concerned about the consequences of this disease, I suggest it would have been much better if the minister had come before the house and said what is the obvious fact, that there has been gross negligence, that gross negligence of that kind is not going to occur again, that we have taken steps to make sure that there will be no similar cases of negligence, that we are going to stop it by having instituted proper supervision of the animals of this country, and that we are going to provide assurance that where there is disease it will be diagnosed.
Progress reported.
I presume it will be the desire of the house to continue with this discussion tomorrow.
